author: Codex
scope: Incremental cached-only assessment. Local subclaims may be resolved while the enclosing uncertainty remains open. No physical manuscript, historical source-book or live-rendering verdict is inferred.

uncertainty_assessments.result: The chapter 5 quotation selects the final two ketiv atoms. The note and appendix explicitly describe Aleppo's single qere note for all three. A partial quotation can coexist with that three-atom statement; whether the chapter intends an exclusive two-atom scope remains editorial. The separately reviewed chapter 2 / two-atom appendix membership case is not a new duplicate finding.

Summary's captured revision predates chapter 2's captured revision, but this does not date the individual sentences. Proverbs 30:19 retains both single and doubled tsinnor helper branches. The current closed projection and local wikitext handler select branch 1. Cached implementation is established; current Hebrew Wikisource visibility is outside this audit.

Both Psalms 66:12 and 119:90 have a space after the quoted first atom in the current raw and selected parsed text. No note addresses that boundary. This resolves current MAM membership only; whether the heading intends a strict maqaf list or broader post-stress-meteg examples, and what Aleppo has, remain open.

2 Kings 14:7's note explicitly names Aleppo for the missing additional pashta, corroborating that narrow subclaim. Its ketiv target remains unpointed, so a complete pointed Aleppo ketiv is not supplied. 2 Samuel 16:23 corroborates the gap/unpointed-qere description with unnamed manuscript wording. No corresponding note exists on the ketiv/qere target at 2 Kings 18:27. Nearby Aleppo notes cannot transfer attribution.

Both sources encode two MUNAH marks, U+05A3, and call them merkha. This is a shared glyph/name anomaly. The cache supplies no basis to choose a corrected physical reading or an author's intended label.

The chapter 2 illustration omits the grey maqaf explicitly prescribed in the same chapter and present in both raw and parsed current MAM. This is a cached policy/illustration difference. Intentional simplification versus stale illustration remains editorial; no manuscript verdict follows.

The central meteg claim agrees. The Introduction's holam differs from the explicit Aleppo quotation and absence explanation. Chapter 2 permits an edition holam; it does not explicitly authorize normalizing manuscript-labelled quotations. The quotation's intended completeness remains editorial.

Both sources address the extra revia. The Introduction also has a vav meteg absent from the note's specimen, but the row has no explicit manuscript sigil for that incidental mark. Neither its Aleppo attribution nor a physical contradiction is established.

The explicit Aleppo quotation lies within the Introduction's declared missing extent. The note supports the grammatical reading from other witnesses and reading tradition. The cache contains no pre-loss Aleppo report or explanation of the sigil's intended shorthand.

The six clauses require separate witness/transcription scope. Deuteronomy 12:30 and Psalm 18:7 distinguish Leningrad from its digital transcription; Psalm 17:14 distinguishes Leningrad alternatives from a reading assigned elsewhere. Daniel 2:41 explicitly allows the digital merkha alternative with וגם זה אפשרי, so it must not be described as a wholly rejected transcription. Daniel 5:3 and Nehemiah 12:47 retain transcription/question qualifiers absent from the Introduction. Physical readings remain unresolved.

The Leningrad note documents the combined munah/merkha form but does not assign each mark to the upper/lower reading strand. Current MAM's two selected strands do not establish Leningrad's strand assignment. Combining-codepoint order is not such evidence.

Song of Songs 4:16's selected/candidate distinction is dagesh on zayin; lamed is undotted in both, so the Introduction's lamed explanation is locally inaccurate. Lamentations 4:7 encodes SEGOL on shin in both specimens while the prose says qamats and preserves uncertainty about close dots. The latter is a shared explanation anomaly, without an independent manuscript reading verdict.

Chapter 4 explicitly defines its star as the selected spelling. It does not assert complete pointing through that star alone. Nehemiah 9:37's missing second telisha and Daniel 7:15's unnamed rejected accent therefore remain incidental quotation questions; the central spelling selections agree.

The spelling evidence agrees, but the cache does not establish every small/large Masorah distinction, specifically small Aleppo Masorah, surprising own-Masorah-L support, or Daniel 5:16's Leningrad ketiv attribution. The sigil decoder explains surprising equality; it cannot supply the missing manuscript fact. Daniel 5:7's parallel note is not evidence for 5:16.

The two incidental meteg specimens retain quotation scope. Numbers 1:10 and 10:19 explicitly document joined/spaced Leningrad forms; whether earlier uncertainty was unwarranted cannot be dated from the cache. Deuteronomy 32:6's Leningrad quotation omits the yod SHEVA explicitly present and described in the note. The holam policy does not explain that SHEVA omission. Joining agrees; complete-quotation intent and physical truth remain open.

Isaiah 44:14's note supplies generic Aleppo Masorah, not specifically small Masorah. Psalm 27:13's six-dot clause explicitly cites small Aleppo Masorah and LS1, not the Introduction's small-L detail. Positive source claims may coexist. Neither absence supplies a contradiction.

Chapter 5 defines its star as the size performed in MAM. All three selected sizes agree. Complete Ruth/Esther targets retain legarmeh and both Psalm 77:8 helper branches retain initial meteg; incomplete survey text must not hide those marks. Full pointing-quotation intent remains editorial.

The implicit leading equality includes Leningrad, while the explanatory yod-meteg witness list names other witnesses. The leading clause could assert absence of the heavy vav rather than every target mark. Neither sigil decoding nor glyph presence resolves that clause scope. The separate PATAH/meteg prose typo remains independently reviewed.

Nine unsigled specimens have explicit Aleppo note counterparts, consistent with the enclosing Aleppo-or-Leningrad heading; missing item sigla are not an evidence block for those nine. Two Jeremiah qere specimens still cross notes documenting ketiv; Ezekiel 17:17's Leningrad claim lacks a matching named-L clause. Inclusion of the additional Proverbs 30:17 Leningrad hataf remains editorial.

Both sources omit the seder from selected MAM and describe Leningrad's internal mark without a list entry. The Introduction hedges its explanation with כנראה but calls Dotan's mark an error; the note preserves doubt. Dotan's source and intended brackets remain outside this cache.

Current MAM has 4465 poetic verses, 2679 DEHI verses and 423 OLEH verses. The current closed MAM-simple disjunctive extractor independently reproduces both memberships; helper/qamats alternatives preserve them. A complete atom-stream predicate partitions the 423 OLEH cases into 368 same-atom and 55 two-atom cases, with zero unmatched cases. All 55 current two-atom verse memberships match the Introduction's three lists exactly: 38 joined by maqaf, 17 spaced. The Introduction's 2685/421 totals still lack a cached source-membership/counting contract. Current cached WLC does not reproduce those totals; its limited scanner recovery is not a complete grammatical census.

Only two of the six existing main targets lacking selected legarmeh are resolved by wrong-reference correction: 2 Samuel 15:2 to 15:30 and Song 3:3 to Ruth 3:3. Song 3:13 to Ruth 3:13 repairs a nonexistent target and is not a third of those six. Four existing selected absences remain: 1 Samuel 11:9, 11:12; Zechariah 10:12; 1 Chronicles 18:10. The historical Wick population and physical witnesses remain unverified. This corrects the maintained research explanation, not Scripture input.

The maqaf is present in both raw and parsed Leningrad ketiv quotations; it is not introduced by the parser. The accompanying prose says no maqaf and the underlying ketiv is unpointed מי אתי with a single qere. Whether the quoted separator reconstructs display or is an error remains unresolved.

Other Introduction passages agree with the notes for Psalm 6:3's qamats, Psalm 74:5's hataf and Psalm 68:18's rafe, while the design lists differ literally. Proverbs 8:34's other entry retains ATNAH HAFUKH and doubt; the design list uses GALGAL and a certain star. These are concrete internal quotation/qualification differences. The central design predicates agree. Complete manuscript-quotation intent and physical readings remain open; do not inflate them into four new central-feature alarms.
